1. Core Clinical Tension: A 42-year-old man presents with new-onset seizures, intermittent severe headaches, and non-communicating hydrocephalus on initial neuroimaging. Contrast-enhanced CT reveals a well-defined rounded intraventricular lesion within the third ventricle accompanied by biventricular and third ventricular dilatation with transependymal CSF transudation. Third ventricular cystic lesions pose a major differential diagnostic dilemma between colloid cysts, ependymal cysts, intraventricular neoplasms (central neurocytoma, subependymoma), and parasitic cysts; intraoperative disappearance followed by postoperative migration into the occipital horn represents an extraordinary clinical phenomenon.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission narrative details the patient's new-onset seizure history (2 episodes over 20 days), 2-week intermittent severe headaches, normal neurologic examination, normal routine blood labs and serum electrolytes, lumbar puncture showing elevated CSF protein (73 mg/dL) with sterile culture and negative HIV serology, and admission non-invasive contrast-enhanced CT showing third ventricular and lateral ventricular hydrocephalus with a rounded CSF-density lesion displaying a punctate enhancing focus in the third ventricle. Confirmatory high-resolution brain MRI identifying the eccentric mural scolex, ventriculostomy exploration, cyst migration, and anthelmintic therapy response are reserved for diagnostic reasoning.
3. Differential Distinctions: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle was considered because of intermittent headaches and third ventricular obstructive hydrocephalus, but colloid cysts typically appear hyperdense on non-contrast CT, are fixed at the foramen of Monro, and do not contain an eccentric enhancing mural nodule (scolex). Intraventricular ependymoma or central neurocytoma causes obstructive hydrocephalus in adults, but typically presents as a solid-cystic enhancing mass with calcifications rather than a purely CSF-density cystic lesion. Intraventricular neurocysticercosis was definitively identified when brain MRI demonstrated an eccentric mural nodule representing the invaginated scolex ('hole-with-a-dot' sign), with subsequent dynamic migration between ventricular compartments.
case_prompt:
A 42-year-old previously healthy man presents to the clinic following two new-onset generalized seizure episodes occurring over the preceding 20 days. He also reports severe, intermittent headaches of 2 weeks' duration. He denies fever, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, or visual disturbances. Systemic review is otherwise negative.

On physical examination, he is afebrile with normal vital signs. Neurologic examination is entirely normal, with intact cranial nerves, normal motor strength and sensory modalities, symmetric reflexes, and no focal neurologic deficits or signs of meningeal irritation.

Initial laboratory evaluation reveals unremarkable routine hematology, normal serum electrolytes, and normal renal function. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis demonstrates an elevated total protein concentration of 73 mg/dL with normal glucose; CSF culture is sterile and HIV serology is negative. A contrast-enhanced cranial CT scan reveals marked dilatation of both lateral ventricles and the third ventricle with prominent subependymal (transependymal) CSF transudation. Within the third ventricle, there is a subtle, well-defined rounded lesion of CSF density containing an internal punctate enhancing focus. The fourth ventricle is normal in caliber, and no intraparenchymal cerebral lesions or skull vault abnormalities are seen.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Colloid Cyst of the Third Ventricle
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because colloid cysts are the most common third ventricular cysts producing intermittent headaches and biventricular hydrocephalus, but colloid cysts are typically hyperdense on CT, situated anterosuperiorly at the foramen of Monro, and lack an internal punctate eccentric mural nodule.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A subtle well-defined rounded lesion was noted within the third ventricle. The lesion was of CSF density and showed a punctate enhancing focus within.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered as potential intraventricular neoplasms obstructing CSF flow, but ruled out because the lesion was purely cystic and CSF-isodense without solid soft-tissue proliferation, tumor vascularity, or broad ependymal attachment.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The lesion was of CSF density and showed a punctate enhancing focus within. The fourth ventricle was normal [Figure 1a]. There were no obvious neuroparenchymal lesions.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The pivotal diagnosis of intraventricular neurocysticercosis with obstructive hydrocephalus was confirmed when brain MRI identified a cystic third ventricular structure containing an eccentric mural nodule corresponding to the parasitic scolex, which subsequently exhibited intraventricular migration into the right lateral ventricular occipital horn following ventriculostomy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: MRI revealed dilatation of the lateral and third ventricles with subependymal transudation of fluid. A cystic structure was seen within the third ventricle, distending it [Figure 1b]. Furthermore, an eccentric mural nodule of intermediate signal intensity was identified. This nodule was thought to represent the scolex.

editor_comments: Case prompt stops at admission triage contrast CT findings without mentioning neurocysticercosis or scolex. Diagnostic reasoning evaluates colloid cyst and neoplasm vs intraventricular NCC, backed by verbatim quotes.
